### D97 — The capacity estimator (M117, 2026-10-06)

The owner, 2026-10-06: "we should also build out an estimator tool where the
user can set a criteria like a milestone to ship or a pr etc and when they
want it done by and this will give an estimate of how many agents you would
need across different devices with the option to spin up the estimate i
imagine a lot of people will use this with vps so the estimator should also
determine what the optimum and minimum setups would be etc and you should be
able to take the same criteria ie milestone pr etc and tell it to estimate a
time line based on maximizing the machines and agents you already have setup
or linked".

**What exists.** The plan's lanes tables carry hour estimates, starts-after
dependencies and a rig (M112 onward in columns; M110 and M111 per phase and
per lane). M113's plan reader (D93.5) reads them under `check:plan`'s
grammar, with git, pull requests and CI as sources (D93.6), and its
determinism rules (D93.1). M116's record keeps the review rounds per module
(D96.1). M107's sampler and governor know each machine's capacity per kind
(D87.4, D87.6); M100 and M110 list the paired devices and nodes; M108's
accounts carry their rate and usage limits (D88.3); M96's board runs lanes on
roles; M109's vault holds credentials as brokered uses (D89.4). Nothing
answers "how long" or "with what".

1. **Two questions, one engine.**
   - **(a) A goal and a deadline:** how many agents, on which machines, and
     the minimum and optimum setups, rented servers included.
   - **(b) A goal and the current fleet:** the timeline when every linked
     machine and agent is used fully.
2. **The goal** is a milestone (`M112`, `12`, `m110a0`, as D93.5 matches), a
   pull request, a set of issues (numbers or a label), a release (the
   milestones the delivery order assigns to it), or a custom list of lanes
   (`M112:Q,U`). Its work comes from M113's reader: each lane's hours, its
   **Starts** dependencies and its rig; open pull requests and their CI from
   M113's sources. Merged lanes are done; a running lane's remainder is its
   estimate less the agent time it has had (M96's board), never below the
   calibrated minimum. A lane's affinity comes from its rig and its files
   (`native/windows/**` needs Windows, `native/darwin/**` macOS, `os/**` a
   Linux builder of its architecture, a GPU lane a GPU).
3. **The fleet.**
   - **Machines:** this machine, M100's paired devices, M110's nodes, and
     rented servers (VPS nodes), each with its OS, architecture, cores, RAM,
     GPU and the user's caps.
   - **Capacity** from M107: concurrent lane slots per machine (its
     governor's capacity per kind, under the user's thresholds), never more.
   - **Agents and accounts:** M96's roles (which kind of lane a role can
     take), and M108's accounts, whose rate and usage limits are hard
     constraints shared by the lanes that use them.
   - **CI:** concurrent jobs and the minutes left in the period, where the
     provider reports them.
4. **History, for calibration.** A journal of past lanes (estimated against
   actual hours, review rounds from M116, CI durations) per lane kind and
   machine class, built from M96's board, git (a lane branch's first commit
   to its merge), M116's record and CI. A documented prior ships
   (`docs/estimator/prior.md`: a lognormal duration around each estimate,
   and review-round rates from this repository's own record) and calibration
   replaces it per kind as the history passes `ESTIMATE_CALIBRATION_MIN_SAMPLES`
   (20 lanes). Below that, the estimate says "uncalibrated prior" in plain
   words.
5. **The engine is deterministic** in D93.1's sense: no model call, no clock
   but the injected `asOf`, the same inputs give the same bytes.
   - **The DAG** of the goal's lanes and their dependencies, with the
     critical path and each lane's slack.
   - **A resource-constrained schedule:** list scheduling, critical path
     first, with machine and slot affinity; each lane also holds its
     account's rate share and its CI jobs.
   - **Review and fix rounds** are drawn from the calibrated rates, with a
     third-strike redesign (D96.1) as a modelled risk on a module that has
     already had two rounds.
   - **P50 and P90 dates** from a seeded Monte Carlo
     (`ESTIMATE_RUNS`, 2,000) over the calibrated distributions, with our
     own small PRNG (no dependency). The seed is the SHA-256 of the canonical
     inputs, or `--seed`, so a run is reproducible.
   - **The limiting resource** is named: machines of a class, slots,
     accounts' rate limits, CI, or the critical path itself, found by
     re-running with each resource class unbounded and naming the one whose
     removal shortens the schedule most. When the critical path binds, it
     says so: more agents would not finish sooner.
6. **Setup recommendations.**
   - **The minimum setup** that meets the deadline at P50, and the one at
     P90; and **the optimum** by cost or by speed (the user chooses): the
     cheapest setup that meets the deadline at P90, or the fastest whose next
     machine would still save at least `ESTIMATE_MARGINAL_FLOOR_HOURS` (4).
   - **Expressed as** N machines of a class (vCPU, RAM, OS, architecture,
     GPU), M agent slots and K accounts, with the marginal value of each
     added machine (P50 and P90 hours saved).
   - **Rented servers** in provider-agnostic size classes
     (`src/shared/machineClasses.json`). An optional price lookup reads public
     provider catalogs that need no account, under M113's network setting,
     cached with its date and shown as "a catalog price on {date}, not a
     quote".
7. **"Spin it up."**
   - **Start lanes now** on the existing fleet: the schedule's first lanes
     are handed to M96's board (and M110's orchestrator hosts) under M116's
     playbook: contracts first and the prerequisite audit before each wave.
   - **Provision rented servers** only through providers the user has
     connected, with their credential held in M109's vault and used by the
     broker against the provider's API origin (D89.4), never seen by the
     estimator.
     - Each server's price and the total are shown first; each spend (each
       server) needs its own explicit confirmation, under a hard budget cap
       the user sets for the run (`estimator.provisionBudgetUsd`, no
       default); a server past the cap is refused.
     - **It never pays and never creates an account** (the owner's rule): a
       provider adapter may call only its allow-listed operations (sizes,
       images, create, status, delete), and never a billing, payment,
       sign-up or account endpoint.
     - The server gets Muse Node OS (where the provider takes a custom image)
       or the container through M110f's cloud-init and rented-server
       installer, and is paired through M110d's routes; until those merge,
       recommendations for rented servers are advice only.
   - **Tear-down** when a provisioned server has been idle
     `ESTIMATE_IDLE_TEARDOWN_MINUTES` (30), after a notice with **Keep**,
     through M110f's teardown and wipe.
8. **Surfaces.**
   - `/estimate <goal> [--by <date>] [--fleet current|minimum|optimum]` in
     every editor's composer, and ACP's `/estimate`.
   - **The Estimator panel:** a Gantt view with the critical path and the
     P50 and P90 marks, the bottleneck callout, the setup cards (current,
     minimum, optimum) with their marginal values, and **Spin it up**.
   - The CLI's `muse-spark-code-acp estimate <goal> [--by …] [--fleet …]
[--format md|html|json|text] [--seed …]`; a TUI view; M113's `estimate`
     report kind.
   - **Re-estimated as lanes finish** (an M115 event trigger on "lane
     finished"), with the drift since the last estimate shown.
9. **Honesty.** Every estimate shows its inputs (lanes, fleet, accounts,
   CI), its calibration sample size per lane kind, its uncertainty (the
   P50–P90 band), and the limiting resource. With too little history it says
   "uncalibrated prior". A price is a dated catalog figure, never a promise.

### D98 — Prompt and chat sharing (M118, 2026-10-06)

Saved prompts live in two scopes, and D98 supersedes D67's storage for them: a
user scope in the agent data folder (`<agentDataFolder>/prompts/v1/`),
available in every workspace, editor and surface, and a workspace scope at
`.muse/prompts/<slug>.md`. An imported prompt is untrusted content: it is
shown in full, never runs by itself, and its variables are listed. Chat
sharing has a conversation-only mode whose filter is an allow-list: it keeps
the item kinds it names and drops every other kind, including one added later.
A confidential workspace refuses to share, and nothing leaves the machine
without a click on the final Share, Copy or Save. Full record:
[docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

### D99 — Broker state transitions (M109 B, 2026-10-06)

Broker core = synchronous reducer + tagged effects. Registration capabilities
bind authentication, requests and connection cleanup to one incarnation.
Each completion carries its operation, connection, incarnation and unlock
generation; stale completions dispose only their own resources. Plaintext is
broker-owned through the final synchronous transport write. Lock advances the
generation and wipes owned buffers before any asynchronous settlement. Audit
writers are isolated resources, with cancellable pending rows and terminal
outcomes that supersede pending work. Audit UI reads capture the installed
writer through a tagged effect, rather than an implicit factory-global reader.
The runner performs I/O; the reducer alone changes broker state. No await-and-recheck implementation remains.

### D100 — Orchestration gotchas become product rules (2026-10-06)

Every gotcha found orchestrating the agent fleet is recorded in
`docs/orchestration-gotchas.md` the session it is found, with the rule that
prevents it and its owning decision; plans and reviews of M96, M96c, M100,
M107, M109, M110, M115, M116, M117 and M120 check it. Each row marked amend
becomes a product rule in its milestone (M96c, M96, M100, M107, M110, M115,
M116, M117, M105) with a named test that fails without it; rows marked covered
stay with D87.14, D90.25, D96, D88 and D97. The lane X placement amendment
recorded here matches D88's: one account per provider per device by default,
and developer options labelled, off by default, badged and audited. Full
record: [docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

### D101 — Evidence-backed agent activity, outcomes and recovery (M119, owner 2026-10-06)

The Agent map and ACP listing separate activity (Active, Waiting with a reason,
Inactive) from ended outcomes (Complete, Incomplete, Failed, Cancelled,
Ended, unverified). Structured evidence alone decides outcomes: normal stop,
budget exhaustion, final check exits, unfinished items, required checks and
worktree state. Missing evidence is unverified; a final message is never parsed
for claims of completeness. Active means an in-flight call/tool or output in a
named short window. Silence does not certify success.

The Agent map and ACP listing separate activity (Active, Waiting with a
reason, Scheduled, Recent, Queued, Blocked-needs-action, Background, Dead)
from evidence (owned conversations, handoffs, tool calls, verification,
errors, cost): activity rows stay live, evidence rows stay inspectable. Full
record: [docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

Receipts are bounded, redacted using existing tool-output redaction and read on
selection within the lazy Agent map budget. They list linked files and line
counts where supplied, commands/check results with exit/duration where supplied,
stop reason and final message. Missing fields are labelled unavailable, never
empty success. Attempts retain prior receipts; recovery never happens
implicitly. Continue includes the receipt's structured reason/unfinished items
followed by the original objective unchanged. Retry starts only from a verified
last commit/start checkpoint in an isolated worktree; otherwise explicit refusal.
All UI strings ship in every translated table. Activity/outcome are text and
outcome changes have a polite announcement. Harness states run in four themes.

### D102 — Outside contributions are vetted before they run or land (2026-10-07)

The owner, 2026-10-07 21:40 PT: "we can keep the pr but we need to vet
people not just admit any code". PR #51, Android/Termux unit tests from an
outside account, was merged on 2026-09-29 by an agent session without his
go. It stays.

1. **Scope.** Every pull request, branch, fork, patch or pasted code not
   authored by the owner or this project's own agent sessions.
2. **The process** is [`docs/contributor-vetting.md`](docs/contributor-vetting.md):
   the person (account age, public repositories and activity, prior pull
   requests and issues, commit identity, linked identity, and the stops);
   the change (every file, with the closest reading for workflows, scripts,
   dependencies and lockfile, native helpers, binaries and generated blobs,
   install hooks, network and process calls, sandbox, permission, approval,
   auth and secret code, weakened or skipped tests, and docs that change
   security guidance or agent instructions); then Codex and Grok reviews
   (never the authoring engine), a record in
   `docs/certification/vetting/pr-N.md`, and the owner's explicit go for
   that pull request and head SHA.
3. **CI.** Workflow runs from forks wait for approval for every external
   contributor (`all_external_contributors`, set 2026-10-07; it was
   `first_time_contributors`, which stopped asking once an author had one
   merged pull request). No run is approved before the change review is
   recorded.
4. **Checkouts.** No outside branch in the main checkout, a shared or lane
   worktree, or a rig with credentials; a throwaway clone without tokens.
5. **No go, no code.** Without the owner's go, agents never merge,
   cherry-pick, copy or reproduce outside code (AGENTS.md rule 16).
6. **Records.** PR #51's retroactive record is
   [`docs/certification/vetting/pr-51.md`](docs/certification/vetting/pr-51.md),
   with a benefit check of its four tests. PR #62, from the same author,
   stays untouched until its own record and the owner's decision.

### D216 — The Model API backend on the Muse Code subscription (C-M95-SUB, 2026-10-10; numbered D106 on its branch until the int/recovery join of 2026-10-23, when that number was found shared with the MCP connector)

**CMSUBKEYR3 redesign (2026-10-10, macmini).** Third review round:
replace independent billing/auth reads with one frozen per-attempt
`BillingRoute` (kind, credential, accountId). Resolve only for Meta-direct
models; other providers keep their origin-bound authentication. Carry the
route through ordinary and compaction guards and transport; the small shared
route module is activation-allowed, explicitly forbidden in headless, and
never added to the nine-byte-slack subscription parser. Compare the
sent credential digest synchronously and re-resolve after durable admission
only to refuse a changed kind/account, never to replace the credential.
The stable subscription identity hashes a fixed label and the resolved,
separator-normalized sign-in path: the captured DEVICE_LOGIN_FILE has no
account/user id, so no uncaptured field or bearer digest is invented.
Rotation preserves saved-session ownership. External paid budget scopes bind
the pasted credential digest separately from the stable conversation owner.
Drop subscription-bound fences
when sign-out leaves an unrelated provider usable; retain pasted-key fences.
Plan exemption, reply cost and runtime accounting use this attempt's route;
clear sending state at completion and never hide the journal with old state.
Subscription readiness refuses with the actual sign-in fix even with a
pasted key. Keep every previously seen secret registered/redacted for the
process lifetime. Paid extras (search, subagents, Auto reviewer) require the
stored pay-as-you-go key and ordinary price/budget/use consent; off features
stay quiet. Extract and test the backend restart predicate. Each of the eight
review findings gets a regression and hash-exact red drill in `m95-sub.md`.
No live/paid calls, dependencies, cap increases or merges. Rig/common rules
assign full quality to the lead; this lane runs scoped suites and static/build
gates directly, with installed hooks on each commit.

The owner, 2026-10-10: users with a Muse Code subscription drive the Model
API backend from their subscription, with no pasted key and no extra
billing; chosen for the fleet too. Lane C-M95-SUB, branch `c/m95-subkey`,
certification [`docs/certification/m95-sub.md`](docs/certification/m95-sub.md).

1. **Credential.** With the one opt-in (`museSpark.useMuseCodeSubscription`
   in VS Code, `--subscription` for `serve`/`exec`), the backend reads the
   subscription key the Muse Code CLI holds after a browser or device-code
   sign-in: `providers.meta`'s `access_token` (the captured `accountLogin`
   shape, `DEVICE_LOGIN_FILE` in `docs/certification/sign-in-detection.md`),
   from the CLI's auth file on every OS (XDG honoured, Windows included),
   read fresh from disk for every attempt: no credential cache supplies a
   later send, and a 64 KiB size guard refuses oversized files before they are
   read. A `muse auth set` file holds a pay-as-you-go `api_key` alone (the
   captured `apiKey` shape) and NEVER counts as the subscription: it reads
   as unsigned and the turn refuses, so a card-billed key is never billed
   as plan. Held in memory only; never displayed, logged, copied
   into settings, sent to telemetry, or written anywhere. The sent key is
   tracked in the shared redactor registry plus exact literals at every
   persistence boundary, so snapshots, logs, receipts and errors redact the
   credential actually sent, retaining old literals until the process ends.
   A 401 surfaces through the ordinary credential-error path.
2. **Tension, for the lead.** D74/M95b reads "another application's client
   or stored tokens are never read or reused", and the research in §4 notes
   subscription credentials are "for use with Muse Code only" (ToS §3.1,
   §10.1(i)). This lane reuses the user's OWN CLI sign-in, with explicit
   opt-in, on the owner's binding order — recorded here so the lead can
   confirm the reading before release.
3. **Refusal, not fallback.** Opted in but missing/unreadable/unsigned (or a
   macOS Keychain pointer, which is never read): the turn refuses with the
   fix; a pasted key is never billed silently. Disabled paid scopes stay quiet.
4. **Billing.** Subscription Meta turns price as plan: usage records carry
   certainty `plan` with no dollar charge, the settle math prices the
   attempt like a plan model (no journal write, no reply-usd, no spend
   accumulation), the dollar session-budget reservation and durable
   preflight are skipped like plan models, headless chat requests admit at
   zero dollars while still counting against `--max-requests`, and the
   runtime daily journal plus run ledger settle $0. Meta plan rows read
   "Muse Code plan" (plan-certainty rows name their provider; any other
   plan row keeps the shared "Plan"); certainty stays one value.
5. **Scope.** VS Code, ACP `serve` and headless `exec` share the core
   resolver. Paid extras bill a stored key: a billed image POST
   authenticates as the pasted key and refuses with the fix when none is
   stored; enabled hosted search, subagents and Auto review use the pasted
   pay-as-you-go key under ordinary price, daily-budget and use consent.
   A search response's model tokens also bill that key, disclosed before use;
   denied search leaves chat on the plan. Off features stay quiet; an enabled
   extra without a pasted key gives the localized refusal. Rotation preserves
   stable session ownership instead of rebinding to a bearer digest; a
   pasted-key switch still refuses. Toggling the opt-in restarts the
   backend and re-reads auth. A refused subscription leaves unrelated
   provider models on their own accounts, including on a living host after
   sign-out; subscription-bound account and budget fences are dropped there. macOS
   Keychain-backed sign-ins refuse with the fix; file-backed sign-ins work
   on Windows, macOS and Linux.
6. **Bundle budget (cap restored, 2026-10-10, RVCMSUBKEY P3-10).** The
   100 → 120 KiB amendment is reverted: the headless preflight reads
   through the run's own bounded reader (parse plus refuse only) instead
   of carrying the key-source class, and `dist/headless.js` measures
   100.0 KiB (102,391 B) against the 100 KiB cap. Cap changes belong to
   the owner.

### D76 — `/legal`: evidence first, fixes only after selection (M97, 2026-10-04)

The `/legal` scan is planned (M97), and its lane writes documentation only.
`/legal` and a command-palette entry run the deterministic scanner locally,
without a model, writes or network, and the report appears before any optional
explanation or repair. The result is facts, not a legal certificate. The
scanner reads manifests, locks and installed metadata across ecosystems
without running their build files. It works offline first, and fetching
missing license metadata is a separate choice. Fixing is optional and bounded,
and begins only after explicit selection and patch confirmation. One scanner,
pure `src/core/legal/` with no `vscode`, serves both backends and CI. Full
record: [docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

The owner asked for a read-only codebase scan of licensing, legal risks and
copyright/header hygiene, followed by recommendations and an optional,
authorized fix phase. **Planned; this lane writes documentation only.** D70–D75
and M91–M96 belong to other drafts; their absence here does not release those
numbers. Research: `docs/certification/m97-research.md`.

- **Two phases, with a real boundary.** `/legal` and a command-palette entry
  run the deterministic scanner locally, without a model, writes or network.
  The report appears before any optional explanation or repair. Scan takes the
  existing Plan-mode hold (M70) only for a live conversation, restored only
  while it still owns that hold. A scan never starts a backend;
  no edit, formatter, hook, verify-loop check, install, build, package-manager
  evaluation or arbitrary shell command runs. Read files directly; any needed
  read-only command must pass the existing admission guard. `legal_scan` never
  exposes a write operation. A skill is guidance, not the security boundary.
  Muse Code's native tools cannot be disabled through `SessionConfig` (D69):
  certify its Plan-mode behavior, including standing allow rules, before a
  model explanation can run. If read-only admission cannot be proved, keep the
  deterministic report available and refuse that explanation with a reason.
- **Facts, not a legal certificate.** A versioned, zod-validated result carries
  stable finding ids, rule/data versions, distribution assumptions, scan scope,
  exclusions, incomplete checks and sorted evidence. Each finding has severity
  (`blocker`, `should-fix`, `advice`), workspace-relative file:line when available,
  package@version and license expression where applicable, its evidence source,
  confidence, explanation, recommendation and fixable flag. Missing evidence
  remains unknown; a heuristic never becomes a proven violation or a clean bill
  of health. Every panel, JSON and requested Markdown export says:
  “not legal advice; for distribution decisions consult a lawyer”.
- **Across ecosystems, without running their build files.** Read manifests,
  locks and installed metadata already present within the chosen workspace;
  cover direct and transitive packages, preserving conflicting evidence.
  Missing locks, unresolved versions, dynamic metadata, absent installed data,
  unsupported lock versions or an unreadable subtree make coverage incomplete.
  No resolver, lifecycle script, `setup.py`, Gradle/Maven plugin or helper is run.

| Ecosystem         | Local evidence to recognize                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| npm / pnpm / Yarn | `package.json`, npm locks, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, Yarn classic/Berry locks, present package license/NOTICE files; absent PnP/install metadata stays unknown                        |
| pip / uv / Poetry | `pyproject.toml`, requirements, `uv.lock`, `poetry.lock`, present distribution `METADATA` and license files; requirements without resolved transitive versions are incomplete |
| Cargo             | `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, present crate manifests, `license` / `license-file` and vendored licenses                                                                         |
| Go modules        | `go.mod`, `go.sum`, `vendor/modules.txt`, present module/vendor license files; checksums alone are not license metadata                                                       |
| Maven / Gradle    | POMs, Gradle declarations/locks and present artifact POM/license metadata; do not evaluate executable build logic                                                             |
| NuGet             | project/package declarations, `packages.lock.json`, `project.assets.json`, present `.nuspec`, license expressions/files                                                       |
| Composer          | `composer.json`, `composer.lock`, present package licenses                                                                                                                    |
| Ruby gems         | `Gemfile`, `Gemfile.lock`, static gemspec declarations and present gem metadata; never execute a gemspec                                                                      |

### D103 — Preferred agents per role, live availability, and lane handoff (M120, 2026-10-08)

The owner, 2026-10-08: "we need to make sure in all of our load balancing
settings we can set preference so some agents are preferred over other when
available for certain roles and can be swapped into and out of lanes
accordingly". This follows from running the fleet. One engine codes faster
than another; one can't run on Windows (muse-code-sdk#96); one is stopped by a
safety classifier on some reviews; one is slow but thorough. A fixed
assignment wastes the fast one, and a fixed "no mid-task move" strands work on
the slow one.

- **One preference model everywhere work is balanced.** Every place the
  product picks who or what runs a piece of work uses the same shape. That
  covers D75 role pools (team workers), M100/M110 device and node routing,
  the judge engine (`museSpark.judge.engine`), M95 provider order
  (`providerOrder`, `allowFallbacks`), and M116 orchestrator dispatch.
  - **A preference list** is an ordered list of **candidates** for a role or
    a lane kind. A candidate is an agent or engine, a model, or a device or
    node, together with its caps (D75: count, task tokens, day tokens) and
    its **conditions**.
  - **Conditions** are capability facts, never vendor names
    (multi-vendor rule): the platform it can run on (Windows-native work
    needs a Windows-capable candidate), the tools and features it supports,
    and role constraints. The built-in constraint is that a **review** role
    never uses the candidate, or the engine, that authored the work. That is
    the owner's "never review with the authoring engine" rule.
- **Preferred when available.** Selection takes the first candidate in order
  that is **available now**, checked live when the task starts:
  - it is signed in and healthy (its last probe succeeded);
  - it is under its caps;
  - it is not rate-limited or cooling down;
  - its device or node is online and admitted by the M107 governor;
  - it meets the task's conditions.
    The panel and the roster show which candidate was chosen, and why each
    earlier one was skipped, in plain words ("Muse: unavailable on Windows
    (sandbox issue)").
- **Swap in and out of lanes (supersedes D75's "no mid-task move").** A
  running task can move to another candidate at a **safe point**. Triggers:
  - **Return to preferred** (on by default): a more preferred candidate has
    become available, and the task is long enough for the move to pay off.
  - **Stall**: no progress (no tool call, file change or commit) for the
    role's stall time.
  - **Time box**: the task has passed its time box.
  - **Cap**: the current candidate reached its cap (D75's "next in line",
    now also applied mid-task).
  - **Refusal**: the current candidate stopped the task. Examples are a
    safety-classifier stop, a crash or a sign-out. The owner's ruling says
    which engine takes a classifier-stopped review.
  - **The user**: "Move to…" on the task, in every editor.
- **The handoff.** The old candidate is stopped, with its whole process tree.
  Its work is then captured:
  - the commits on the task branch;
  - the uncommitted diff, binary-safe;
  - the new files;
  - a short progress note taken from its transcript.
    Nothing is stashed, and no hook is skipped. The new candidate gets the
    original brief, the captured work, and an instruction to review that
    work critically before continuing. The task's report records the chain
    of candidates, with the trigger and time of each move. Meters and spend
    stay with the candidate that used them.
- **Specialized coding roles (owner, 2026-10-08).** "for the coding roles we
  need to be able to setup front end coders and backend coders because some
  agents are better at certain tasks".
  - **D75's single `engineering` role becomes a family:**
    - `frontend`: UI, webviews, CSS, accessibility, visual receipts;
    - `backend`: host, core, runtime, protocols, storage, money;
    - `engineering`: kept as the general or full-stack role, and the
      fallback for both.
      Each role has its own charter, tools, caps and preference list, so the
      user can put one agent first for front-end work and another for
      back-end work.
  - **Routing a task to the right specialist.** Each coding role's charter
    carries **area hints**: path globs (`src/webview/**`, `**/*.css`,
    `src/host/**`) and plain-word kinds ("UI layout", "protocol"). The
    orchestrator picks the role whose hints match the task's planned files
    and description.
    - A task that spans both is split into one lane per area when the parts
      are separable, joined by the lead.
    - When it can't be split, it goes to the role covering most of it, and
      a review is added from the other specialist. That reviewer must still
      differ from the author.
    - The roster shows why a role was chosen ("12 of 14 planned files under
      `src/webview`").
  - **Users add more specializations** the same way as other roles: an
    `AGENT.md` with its area hints, for example `native` (Swift, C#, C),
    `tests`, `docs`, `data` or `infra`. A project copy may only narrow a
    built-in role (D75 role keys).
  - **Which agent is better at what is learned, not guessed.** The panel
    keeps per-role, per-candidate outcomes:
    - first-review acceptance;
    - findings by severity;
    - rounds to acceptance;
    - time;
    - redesigns.
      It **suggests** a reorder when one candidate is clearly better for a
      role ("Muse: 4 of 5 front-end tasks accepted on first review; Codex: 1
      of 4"). It never reorders on its own unless the user turns on
      auto-order for that role.
- **Defaults keep today's behaviour.** With no team and no custom
  preference (the single-model user), nothing is swapped and nothing
  changes. Swaps apply only between configured candidates.
- **Every editor.** The preference editor (drag to order; per candidate:
  caps and conditions; per role: stall time, time box, return-to-preferred)
  and "Move to…" exist in VS Code, JetBrains, Visual Studio, Eclipse and the
  companion (all editors are equal).
- **Fleet first.** The lead's own rig orchestration already follows these
  rules. `scratchpad/rig-lanes/roles.json` holds the preference lists, and
  the handoff is the one used on 2026-10-08 (Codex → Muse and Codex →
  Claude, with the saved diff). Its gotchas go into
  `docs/orchestration-gotchas.md`.

### D104 — Git and pull requests in every editor (M123, 2026-10-08)

M123 brings M71's Git and pull requests (F36) to every editor. Git runs
natively in the shared runtime with the user's own `git` under M107's
admission and no deadline of ours (VS Code keeps its Git extension); M71's
rules carry over (never force, push and pull requests ask, a commit never
pushes); only the confirmed push and the pull request fetch get the user's
allow-listed Git environment, and each mutation is one bound plan, confirm,
lock, revalidate, spawn pipeline. GitHub stays on M71's REST client; the token
comes from, in order, the editor's sign-in by lease, the runtime's OAuth
device flow (kept in the vault) or an opt-in `gh` login, with `repo` scope
only. Drafts, links and checkout of others' pull requests go through the
shared panel, held by location in every host. D4 names these sources;
GitHub.com only; registering the OAuth App is the owner's (Q-M123). Full
record: [docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

### D105 — Windows trusted paths: a trusted root, links above it by identity (TRUSTROOT, 2026-10-09)

**Owner rule (2026-10-08, "Windows paths: any drive").** Profile folders may
be junctions or symlinks, or redirected to another drive; never assume `C:`.
Links above a trusted root are normal and are accepted by comparing resolved
identity; links inside the trusted tree that escape it are refused at the
first escaping component.

**Decision (lead, 2026-10-09).** `windowsTrustedPathVerifier` used OpenSSH
`safe_path` over the whole path: every component up to the drive root was
ACL-checked and any reparse point anywhere was refused, so native schedules
and helpers refused a relocated profile. It now verifies against a trusted
root, the folder the caller owns (`TrustedPathVerifier.verify` takes
`root`; omitted, it is the file's own folder, or the folder itself):

Owner rule (2026-10-08, Windows paths: any drive): profile folders may be
links; links at and above a trusted root are accepted by resolved identity,
links inside that escape are refused. Lead decision (2026-10-09): the verifier
checks against the owned root by identity, never string prefix. Full record:
[docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

Native schedule callers pass no root: each launcher, script, record and
definition is trusted from its own folder (the record's folder is the
schedule data directory). Evidence: `test/unit/windowsTrustedPath.test.ts`
(profile junction above the root, the root itself a junction, escaping and
in-tree junctions below it, drive-letter spelling) and
`docs/certification/trustroot.md`.

### D106 — Muse Spark Code as an MCP connector for other agents (M124, 2026-10-07)

The owner, 2026-10-07: "is there a way to add this in some capacity also as a
connector for openai, anthropic, meta, gemini etc so it can add the functionality
to those agents directly?" **Yes: expose the harness's functions as MCP tools.**
The other agent keeps its own model and conversation; Muse Spark Code
(Unofficial) supplies orchestration, evidence, advice, reports, schedules and
prompt sharing under the user's own permissions. This grants no access to a
vendor's subscription, private agent state or credentials.

The dated primary-source matrix, proposed input schemas, scopes, approval
state machine, safety rules and qualification plan are in
[`docs/design/mcp-connector.md`](docs/design/mcp-connector.md). Research was
read on 2026-10-07; product availability is documented, not tested here.
**The owner, 2026-10-09: the local phase starts now; the hosted phase
(ChatGPT/claude.ai OAuth over HTTPS) waits for M110, the orchestrator-link
contract and a domain/OAuth choice.** M124 is in progress on the local stdio
phase; nothing here claims that a connector ships.

1. **One local entry.** Add `muse-spark-code-acp mcp` to the existing
   standalone runtime, serving MCP over stdio in a lazy bundle. ACP remains
   its own protocol mode. Configuration contains no key. An owner-created
   local connection grant binds workspaces and tool families; launching the
   process or trusting a repository never grants write authority. No general
   shell, file-system, credential, OAuth-admin or approval-answer tool.
2. **Useful, bounded tools.** Fleet and Agent map status; D101/M119's
   outcomes and receipts; start, continue and Stop for lanes and teams; M116's
   deterministic placement advice; M117's capacity estimate; M113's
   deterministic `/report`; M115's schedule list/create/update/cancel; M118's
   prompt library and previewed sharing. Read tools never start checks,
   provision servers, refresh paid data, save exports or run prompts. Missing
   dependencies say `unavailable`, never return empty success. No guessed
   provider frame or outcome field. D101/M119's portable outcome mapping and
   receipts shipped in 0.16.0, but they live inside the running session (the
   Agent map, ACP `/agents`): no cross-process outcome store exists that the
   connector's separate process can read, so those tools say `unavailable`
   until their owner exports one.
3. **Remote on the home node.** M110 serves the same registry over HTTPS
   Streamable HTTP. That phase needs three things, none of which exists yet:
   (a) M110's home node (D90; planned, nothing implemented); (b) the
   paired-node link of D90.8, D80.3's bounded, versioned session protocol over
   pinned mutual TLS 1.3 (M100; planned); and (c) an orchestrator-link command
   contract: how a home node forwards a connector intent, its approval (D90.3,
   through D90.10's approval forwarding), identities, epochs, ownership and
   revocation to the orchestrator. No PLAN decision or source defines (c). It
   is a dependency owned by M110 lane 0's threat model and contracts, not
   something M124 invents; M124 adds neither a second scheduler nor a guessed
   link wire shape.
4. **OAuth for hosted chats.** ChatGPT and claude.ai get OAuth 2.1 discovery,
   authorization code plus PKCE, audience-bound tokens, scoped grants and
   revocation. Support published client metadata (CIMD), static registrations
   and DCR for clients needing it; DCR is not universally required and the
   current MCP spec deprecates it in favor of CIMD. Scope each connection to
   named workspaces and target devices; consent to linking, disclosure and
   each action are separate. OAuth tokens never become Model API keys or
   paired-node credentials and never reach tools or child environments.
5. **Our UI decides.** Every write, run, paid or physical operation requires
   the user's approval in **our host UI**, including when the calling client
   uses Always allow, Auto or Bypass. Arguments, MCP elicitation, remote chat
   confirmations and tool annotations cannot answer it. The shared host
   bridge carries a one-use decision bound to the principal, payload, target,
   generation, price and expiry; changes or missing UI refuse. Paid uses keep
   D30/D48's price, budget, consent and tally; connector paid grants default
   off. No approval-answer tool exists.
6. **Stop never asks.** Authorized Stop and schedule cancellation have a
   reserved path independent of the approval queue, ordinary call limits,
   spending and kill switch. Ownership/authentication still apply; Stop never
   means stopping another user's work. An unreachable worker remains unknown
   until its receipt arrives. D83's fixed machine Stop may join when its owner
   certifies it; no machine payload or other physical tool joins M124.
7. **D83 survives delegation.** No physical connect, program or actuate in
   remote lanes, teams, schedules, headless or CI; refused operations stay
   refused in every mode. A parent run approval never approves a nested
   physical or paid action. Stop remains D83's fixed out-of-band sequence.
8. **Disclosure and audit.** Return allow-listed projections through the
   existing shared redaction owner, including registered values, account/path
   scrub and a final whole-result scrub. Never return raw logs, environments,
   credentials or unrestricted artifacts. Every call, rejection and outcome
   has a scrubbed audit receipt. Tool output and imported prompts are untrusted
   data. Bound frames, results, polls, pending approvals, run capacity and
   budgets; fail closed on audit failure except Stop. A local kill switch
   rejects new effects, invalidates pending approvals/grants and cancels
   connector-owned work, keeping authenticated Stop available.
9. **All editors equal.** Shared core/runtime, shared React approval UI and
   M104's host bridge, with the authenticated companion page when an editor
   cannot display it. VS Code/VSCodium/Theia/code-server, Cursor/Windsurf, Zed,
   JetBrains, Visual Studio, Eclipse, Xcode, Neovim/Emacs/Sublime and ACP/TUI
   hosts get the same registry and host authority. Native MCP support varies;
   a host without it uses an MCP-capable external agent plus our companion UI.
   A missing UI denies effects explicitly, never grants lesser protection.
10. **Qualification by product.** Local stdio first; hosted HTTP after
    decision 3's three dependencies. OpenAI's Apps SDK/connector docs now
    route to plugin docs; optional embedded UI is not an approval authority.
    Gemini CLI, Gemini Apps and Gemini Enterprise/ADK are separate rows. Meta
    AI connectors are early access with unspecified public transport/limits,
    so qualification waits for access and docs. No vendor endorsement,
    account registration, paid call or publication is authorized by this
    decision. M124's delivery updates README, CHANGELOG, PRIVACY, SECURITY,
    ACP docs and the generated Help reference.

### D107 — The Judge: our own Jev, for speed and accuracy (M125, 2026-10-09)

The Judge (M125) is our own Jev-style engine: one call per state answers every
due question with calibrated probabilities, to make the agent faster and more
accurate, never a layer on top. Engines rank by measured speed and
calibration, the chat model last and never inline; one eligibility function
admits an engine per timing class (inline, slack, boundary, post-turn), and
misses suspend it. By the 2026-10-10 bench ruling Jev online stays the engine,
and no local engine vetoes until a calibrated one shows about zero unsafe
approves and accuracy within 2 points of Jev. The Set Up Local Judge wizard is
in every editor. Off and all-abstaining are byte-identical; a decision is on
by default only when measured wins hold without slower turns; the judge never
answers the user, writes code or alone grants an action. The owner's approval
fast path (Q-D107 B): a held Auto action skips the reviewer only past the
deterministic floor, in B1 (inspect, Linux and macOS) or B2 (check scripts,
Linux) confinement, with no veto within 5 s; nothing skips until a fitted
profile lands, and a class is on by default only after zero harm in 400
labelled actions. It supersedes D77's `auto` resolution and ready-rate rule.
Full record: [docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

### D117 — A provider's refusal reads as the provider's refusal (lane PROVERR, 2026-10-12; numbered D108 until 2026-10-17, when that number was found shared with the test overhaul)

**Rule in force.** A provider's answered refusal is one typed value
(`ProviderRefusal`: HTTP status, closed kind, the provider's bounded words,
its request id and its wait), parsed per wire format, never replaced by a
product sentence. The person reads one sentence built from the kind in every
host and language, naming the provider with its own words after it.
`modelsPanelUnavailable` is raised only where a part of the build is truly
missing (the models-panel bundle loader). A refusal answered with a 4xx
status before processing (`isDefiniteRefusal`: 400, 401, 402, 403, 404, 413,
422, 429) releases its reservation in full — settled 0, uncertain 0;
anything else (5xx, 408/409, unanswered) keeps its uncertain liability.
Never retried: credit, authentication, permission, notFound, invalidRequest,
tooLarge; rateLimited and overloaded follow the retry tables that exist.
A failure before anything was written is "could not reach \<provider\>";
after a write belongs to the transmission branch
(`fix/stream-limits-class-r5`). The ledger branch (`fix/spend-ledger`) owns
everything past the definite-refusal decision. Full record:
`docs/certification/provider-refusals.md`.

- **Archived.** The record that stood here is in [docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

### D118 — Refusals read by shape, retried by code, stored without leaks (lanes PROVERR round 2 + PROVERRR2, 2026-10-13; numbered D109 until 2026-10-17, renumbered with D117)

One extractor reads an error body by what it IS, whatever the wire format; the
status and the provider's documented type, code or reason decide the kind, a
phrase only where a recorded answer shows the provider gives nothing else.
Retry follows the preset's own table with the envelope code (a quota 429 never
retries while a bare one does); Anthropic max_tokens maps as documented.
Parity: a bad key reads authentication at all eleven recorded providers, an
unknown model reads notFound at all twelve. Full record:
[docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

**Amended 2026-10-17 (lane PROVERRORS, from the provider research of PR
#202).** A provider's wait is honoured as given in every form it uses
(`retry-after-ms`, then `Retry-After` seconds or date): no cap of ours
refuses it and the backoff never shortens it. Each preset retries by its
provider's own rule (OpenRouter: 429, 503 and the in-flight-budget 402;
Gemini adds 408), and a retryable error a stream ends with before any
content is sent again as its status would be. A provider's own codes decide
the kind: Z.ai's 1308-1321, OpenRouter's budget limit sources and Gemini's
`quota_exceeded` are usage limits, never retried, with the provider's words
(and the reset they name) quoted. Our own refusals (a budget or ledger
stop, a lapsed confirmation, a codec refusal) pass through the provider
path unchanged and are never retried; only a failure with a connection
code in its causes is a send failure, retried as one and reported with
Node's codes and the send's unknown fate; a connection lost after the 200
says so. Every refusal sentence carries the provider's request id. The
retry count, the backoff bounds and the idle timeout stay as they are
pending the owner's decision (evidence in
`docs/certification/provider-refusals.md`, "Lane PROVERRORS").

**Amended 2026-10-17 (lane RETRYLIMITS, owner's binding rule).** The single
global retry count (4) and backoff (1 s to 60 s) are replaced by each
provider's documented values (`docs/certification/provider-refusals.md`,
"Lane RETRYLIMITS"): Anthropic 2 (SDK default), OpenAI 2 (SDK default;
review RVRETRYLIMITS), Gemini 4 with ~1 s to 60 s
(SDK), Azure up to 10 (top of its documented 5–10 example range), xAI up to
4 retries (5 attempts, 2^attempt s), Meta 4 (3–5 attempts). Anything a
provider does not document is the person's `museSpark.modelApiMaxRetries`
setting, unset by default; with none set the provider's own Retry-After
(or stop answer) governs, with no cap of ours. The idle timeouts stay as
they are (not this lane).

**Cause.** Round 1 classified 11 of 23 recorded real answers wrong (the red
table): typeless 401s read as "unrecognised", xAI/Mistral/Gemini shapes
unread, quota-worded limits retried, spend caps retried, cut-off Anthropic
replies ending the turn. The scans then showed the same defect from the
other side: error bodies replaced by one fixed sentence on the configured
path. Full record: the round-2 certification and the gap certifications.

### D120 — The terminal agent documents itself per command (lane CLIHELP, 2026-10-12; numbered D117 on the release train until the main-now merge of 2026-10-17, renumbered for main's D117, then D120 at the 0.19.0 join when D119 was found shared with the three-valued-reads decision)

One table drives the terminal command parser and installed-language help.
`<command> --help` and `help <command>` print that command's own help; `help --all`
/ `help reference` retain the full reference. Wrong options and values exit 2
with accepted options/values, without echoing secret-looking names. `providers
models <entry>` edits models through the validated atomic provider-file
commit; forced additions retain a reason and never read a key. The reference
gate checks registry coverage and the README terminal topics. The thirteen
help topics cover the registry routes except `estimate`; older non-registry
grammars retain their own usage and are not help topics. Proof:
`docs/certification/cli-help.md`. Full record:
[docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md) (archived
as D117; the number changed only, the record stands).

### D119 — Reads that guard money, consent or credentials are three-valued (2026-10-12; numbered D109 until 2026-10-17, when that number was found shared)

A read that guards money, consent or a credential answers found, absent,
or could-not-read with a closed kind — never a boolean that collapses the
third state into absence. Guards fail closed on could-not-read (a billing
hold is never released, a sign-in never lifts one, "can recover" is never
true, no key is asked for as if none existed) and tell the person once per
distinct damage through a notice, not only the log. Full record:
`docs/certification/catch-money.md` (round 3).

### D207 — Money and consent failures reach the person in words (lead, 2026-10-16; numbered D119 until the 0.19.0 join, when that number was found shared with D119 three-valued reads)

The estimator's own refusal keeps its detail in words (`estimateFailureText`); anything else reads failed without its raw text. A foreign typed failure keeps its kind past each boundary with its cause, and only the current run reports. The worded-refusal matcher (`isEstimateRefusal` / `estimateRefusalDetail`) tells the estimator's own words apart from anything else. Proof: `test/unit/estimateRefusal.test.ts`, `test/unit/estimatorSurfaces.test.tsx`.

### D108 — Test overhaul: no stand-ins, a short gate, the real-life run (owner, 2026-10-12)

The owner, verbatim: "get the useless tests get it streamlined and
meaningful with nothing testing fake code no exceptions. no more ci
screenshot runs. if we change the ui is gets a small local verification
and thats it." A thousand-test suite kept shipping broken code as
"completed", so the suite is overhauled, not extended.

The owner, verbatim: get the useless tests, streamline it, and prove the gate
short. A test stays only if it runs real code (no stand-ins, no fakes, no
screenshot or frame comparison); no coverage gate; the short gate and the
real-life run are the proof. Full record:
[docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).

### D122 — CI capacity from a second account; the project stays here (owner, 2026-10-16; redesigned 2026-10-17)

**D122 — The capacity repository runs every Windows and macOS job (static
gates, unit shards, Windows integration, the macOS dictation helper, the
Hosts/Forks checks and the Windows/macOS browser captures); the project, its
pull requests and main stay on the owner's account.** While
`ORG_CI` is `on` and the organization GitHub App's key
(`ORG_CI_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`, which GitHub never gives a fork's or Dependabot's
run) reaches a same-repository pull request's full-tier run, that run is part
`home`: build.yml's `org` job pushes the merge commit to
`scnetsolutions/muse-spark-code-ci` as `ci/pr-<number>` with a one-hour token
for that repository alone (contents and workflows write), the same workflows
run every Windows and macOS leg there (part `org`), and `org`
succeeds only if that run did; the macOS helper artifacts come back through
`org` for the `packages` job. The seven required names fold in its result, so
the ruleset is unchanged; every other run keeps every job here (part `all`).
The Windows static gates and the Windows browser capture take the
larger runner there while that repository's `LARGE_RUNNERS` variable is
`on` (owner, 2026-10-18, $40 monthly budget backstop); macOS stays standard
(the GitHub-owned macOS larger labels need a Team or Enterprise plan and
the capacity organization is free). Test shards stay on
free standard runners. The capacity repository stays public and holds no
secret. Owner setup:
CONTRIBUTING.md, "The capacity repository (D122)"; proofs:
`docs/certification/ciflow.md` (D122, CISHARDS2). Full record:
[docs/plan-archive/decisions.md](docs/plan-archive/decisions.md).
